structure.title: Books I–II · The cell and its unruly occupant
structure.text: Brief chapters move from public esteem, talk and learning to the cultivation of an inward life. A person who has withdrawn from the world can still spend an afternoon wishing the world would hear about it.

structure.title: Book III · A disciple listens and answers
structure.text: Instruction becomes intimate dialogue. A disciple brings discouragement, temptation and the desire for comfort before Christ. The returns to familiar troubles give devotion a duration beyond the moment of a strong feeling.

structure.title: Book IV · Approaching the altar
structure.text: Communion gives the earlier questions of humility and desire a particular place and time. The person preparing to receive Christ has to speak about love, unworthiness and longing within the same prayer.

people.name: The disciple
people.role: A voice learning how to ask
people.text: The disciple wants divine consolation and also wants to know how to live when it recedes. Hearing both wishes makes the prayers more vulnerable than a list of maxims about detachment.

people.name: The inward voice of Christ
people.text: The dialogue lets a searching or corrective answer stand beside the disciple's own account. Sometimes the wish for praise survives in the very achievement the disciple offers as evidence of humility.

context.title: A devotional book shaped by common life
context.text: The advice grew out of a religious setting in which meals, silence and obedience involved actual neighbours. A rebuke about tolerating somebody's faults can concern the person one is about to meet again at dinner.

notice.text: Notice what occupies the mind in solitude.
notice.why: An imaginary admirer is enough to turn inward practice into a performance. The book gives considerable attention to intentions that survive the disappearance of an audience.

notice.text: Follow the changing meaning of comfort.
notice.why: Sometimes comfort is a gift gratefully received. Sometimes the demand to keep feeling it becomes a new attachment. The difference matters whenever a prayer seems to go unanswered.

opening: It is possible to become learned about humility, speak beautifully about devotion, and still spend the day wanting people to admire you. Thomas à Kempis has little patience for that arrangement. His instructions bring Christianity into the private territory where vanity survives its own exposure: resentment at correction, pleasure in praise, the wish to appear holy. Written for a life of devotion, this book asks for changes that are difficult to display and offers a companionship intended to endure when admiration disappears.
